titre: Schrödinger's Cat Was an Objection, Not a Thesis
accroche: Erwin Schrödinger never claimed that a cat could be both alive and dead: he wanted to prove that the idea was absurd.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1935, the Austrian physicist Erwin Schrödinger imagines a cat locked in a steel chamber, with a vial of hydrocyanic acid, a hammer mechanism, and a tiny amount of radioactive substance linked to a Geiger counter. If a single atom decays within the hour, the mechanism breaks the vial and the cat dies. Otherwise, it lives. The general public has taken away a mistaken idea: that quantum mechanics claims the cat is, before anyone looks, both alive and dead.

## An Objection, Not a Proposal

Schrödinger proposes nothing of the kind. A few months earlier, he had received a letter from Einstein comparing a similar situation to a keg of gunpowder in unstable chemical equilibrium, which may or may not have exploded without anyone knowing. Schrödinger takes up the idea and pushes it to the point of absurdity with an animal, precisely to attack the Copenhagen interpretation: if one takes seriously the idea that a quantum system remains in a superposition of states as long as no one observes it, and one couples this system to a macroscopic object through a physical mechanism, then one would have to accept that an entire cat also ends up in an indeterminate state. Schrödinger himself calls this consequence “quite ridiculous.”

His paper, published in three installments in the journal Die Naturwissenschaften in late 1935, is a critical text, not a research hypothesis. The cat serves only to make visible, at the scale of an everyday object, what the mathematical abstraction of superposition conceals at the atomic scale.

## What the Legend Turned Upside Down

The phrase “the cat is both alive and dead” has come to circulate as if it summed up what quantum physics actually claims. It is the opposite of its author's intention: Schrödinger wanted to show that a theory leading to such a conclusion, applied carelessly to a macroscopic object, has something unacceptable about it, not that it should be accepted.

The debate Schrödinger wanted to open is, moreover, still not closed. A century later, the question of exactly where and why the quantum world gives way to the familiar macroscopic world, the one where cats are, unambiguously, alive or dead, remains one of the open problems of fundamental physics. The cat continues to serve as the example in every discussion of measurement in quantum mechanics, not because it describes a reality, but because it makes the question impossible to dodge.

repere.texte: Published in three installments in Die Naturwissenschaften in late 1935, the thought experiment was never presented by Schrödinger as a serious hypothesis: he himself calls its consequences “quite ridiculous,” to demonstrate the absurdity of applying the Copenhagen interpretation literally to a macroscopic object.
repere.source: Erwin Schrödinger, “Die gegenwärtige Situation in der Quantenmechanik,” Die Naturwissenschaften, 23, 1935 — qualifier reported by PBS NOVA, “Many Worlds”

carte.punch: Schrödinger never thought a cat could be both alive and dead.
carte.idee: In 1935, Schrödinger imagines a cat coupled to a quantum mechanism to mock the Copenhagen interpretation, not to defend it. He himself calls the consequence, a cat “both alive and dead,” “quite ridiculous.” Popular legend has reversed his intention.

quiz.question: Why did Schrödinger imagine a cat both alive and dead in 1935?
choix: To propose a laboratory experiment that could actually be carried out
To illustrate a new calculation method in quantum mechanics
To prove that cats, like particles, exist in superposition
To show the absurdity of applying superposition to a macroscopic object
quiz.explication: Schrödinger criticizes the Copenhagen interpretation; he does not defend it: by coupling a quantum system to a macroscopic object, he shows that a literal application of superposition leads to a consequence he himself judges “quite ridiculous.”

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the imagined setup, what triggers the cat's death?
choix: The experimenter opening the steel chamber
The decay of a single atom, detected by a Geiger counter
A full hour going by, whatever happens inside the box
A physicist outside the box observing the cat
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A tiny amount of radioactive material is linked to a Geiger counter: if a single atom decays within the hour, a hammer mechanism breaks the vial of hydrocyanic acid. It is this coupling between a quantum event and an ordinary object that makes up the whole argument.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What comparison had Einstein proposed a few months earlier?
choix: A keg of unstable gunpowder, exploded or not without anyone knowing
A thrown die whose visible face no one yet knows
A clock whose mechanism stops at the instant of measurement
A cat locked in a box with a vial of poison
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Einstein writes to Schrödinger in 1935, comparing the situation to a keg of gunpowder in unstable chemical equilibrium. Schrödinger takes up the idea and pushes it further by coupling it to an animal, which makes the absurdity impossible to dodge.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How was the 1935 text published?
choix: As an open letter addressed to Niels Bohr
All at once, in a Viennese popular-science magazine
In three installments in the journal Die Naturwissenschaften
In the proceedings of a conference held in Copenhagen the same year
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The paper appears in late 1935 in three successive installments in Die Naturwissenschaften. It is a critical text, addressed to the community of physicists, and not a research hypothesis that Schrödinger wanted to see put to the test.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which problem does the entry present as still open today?
choix: Whether the cat in the experiment would actually have survived
Which of Einstein or Schrödinger came up with the idea of the cat
How to build a Geiger counter sensitive enough
Where the quantum world gives way to the macroscopic world
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A century later, the boundary between the domain where superposition holds and the one where cats are unambiguously alive or dead remains an open problem of fundamental physics. The cat is still used as an example for that reason, not because it would describe a reality.
